If. See Taz in Yoreh De'ah, siman 266, seif 11, where Taz discusses the matter at length. Rama there rules that where there is uncertainty whether an infant is a 7-month or an 8-month child, even if his hair and nails are not fully developed, the brit milah is performed because either he is a viable 7-month child and the mitzvah applies, or he is an 8-month nonviable child and cutting his flesh is of no consequence. Taz, however, writes that one should not be lenient. Regarding desecrating Shabbos to save such an infant, certainly one does not desecrate Shabbos where he is of doubtful 7- or 8-month status and his hair and nails are not complete; see Shach there, seif katan 15. This implies that rabbinic prohibitions may nevertheless be performed by a Jew, just as the brit milah itself is performed under the either-or reasoning, even though moving the child is rabbinically prohibited. One should not argue that moving is lighter, for wounding involves the melacha of extracting, and although where the blood itself is not needed the prohibition is rabbinic, it is nevertheless a rabbinic prohibition, yet the act is permitted because a rabbinic doubt is treated leniently for the mitzvah of brit milah, since perhaps he is a 7-month child. The same reasoning should apply to rabbinic acts for pikuach nefesh.

See Even HaEzer, siman 4, Beit Shmuel, letter 19, regarding the rule that a child is sometimes treated as a 7-month child even where only 5 calendar months separate the relevant dates. The same can affect the Shabbos calculation. Regarding a woman who gives birth in the ninth month there is a dispute there. It is possible that brit milah presents no Torah-level concern because of the either-or argument and a rabbinic doubt is treated leniently; the matter requires study.

Regarding a doubtful 7- or 8-month child whose hair and nails are incomplete on the second day of Yom Tov in the Diaspora, the matter likewise requires study. See Shach, Yoreh De'ah siman 266, seif katan 8, who inclines to say that even a doubtful case overrides the second day of Yom Tov. All the more so here, where there is an either-or argument and perhaps the halacha follows Rama there in seif 11.

If a child of doubtful 7- or 8-month status is born already lacking a visible foreskin and requires only hatafat dam brit, there may be a Torah-level issue of extracting blood because the blood itself is needed for the mitzvah. This resembles wounding for a therapeutic purpose, and one must analyze Rambam, chapter 8, concerning wounding where the blood is desired, as well as the discussion in Kesubos where the act is considered extracting even though the blood is not desired for its own sake but for determining a fact. This may remove the either-or basis for leniency on the second day of Yom Tov.

Know also that brit milah overrides tzaraat, as ruled in Yoreh De'ah, siman 266. In a doubtful 7- or 8-month child the same either-or logic can apply because if he is an 8-month nonviable child the cutting is legally insignificant. It requires study whether those whose brit milah does not override Shabbos, such as one with 2 foreskins or an androgynos, nevertheless have tzaraat overridden for their brit milah.

Taz in siman 588, seif katan 5, writes that where the Torah explicitly permits an act on Shabbos by the word 'day,' the Sages have no power to decree against it, for 'on the day' implies even Shabbos or Yom Tov. Otherwise one could have said that 'day' comes only to include Yom Tov. See there and Tosefet Shabbos.

One who was born without a visible foreskin and is of doubtful 7- or 8-month status is not treated leniently on Shabbos according to Rama in Yoreh De'ah, siman 266, seif 11. One cannot create a double doubt in favor of leniency, because even if he is an 8-month child, the act of drawing covenantal blood is not automatically free of prohibition, while if he is a 7-month child perhaps there is no hidden foreskin. At minimum there remain rabbinic concerns rather than a true double doubt toward permission.

Everything the Mechaber writes in seif 5 concerning cases whose brit milah does not override Shabbos applies likewise to Yom Tov.

Shach in Yoreh De'ah, siman 262, letters 1 and 2, seeks to prove from Menachos 72a that one who performed brit milah before the eighth day must, after the fact, perform the mitzvah again, because otherwise why would brit milah override Shabbos? This proof requires consideration, for one who acts before the eighth day has certainly failed to fulfill the positive commandment 'on the eighth day,' whereas in the Menachos case the essential mitzvah was accomplished and only the preferred time element was lacking. Moreover, the Scriptural derivations concerning harvesting and brit milah are not identical. Brit milah is especially weighty, being associated with 13 covenants and having an explicit Scriptural permission.

I was uncertain whether one who intentionally performed a brit milah not at its proper time on Yom Tov receives lashes. Shabbos 133a states that Yom Tov contains both a positive and a negative commandment and that a positive commandment does not override both. It is possible that the mitzvah nevertheless overrides the negative commandment itself, leaving only the positive commandment of Yom Tov, in which case there would be no liability for lashes and the person might remain qualified for testimony. The Yerushalmi at the end of Lulav HaGazul, and the discussions of the authorities concerning whether a positive commandment overrides the Shabbos prohibition in exceptional configurations, bear on this question. The matter has many ramifications and requires further study.

Twilight. Bach writes in Yoreh De'ah, siman 266, that if the infant was born one twenty-fourth of an hour before the appearance of 3 medium stars, the brit milah is performed on Friday, whereas if he was born later it is doubtful and the brit milah is deferred until Sunday. Although Bach wrote in siman 261 that one should be stringent to accept Shabbos from the end of the 22nd hour, he says that the law of brit milah is different.

This requires study, because Bach himself ruled in Yoreh De'ah that twilight begins 3 quarters of a mil before nightfall, and it is well known that this is less than a quarter-hour, as stated in siman 459. Perhaps he erred in haste and thought that it was 3 mil. The primary ruling is as stated in Yoreh De'ah, siman 266, seif 9, that from the end of sunset the time is doubtful. This is 3 quarters of a mil, as explained in siman 261, approximately a quarter-hour before nightfall. If the child was born before that point, the brit milah is performed on Friday, for even with respect to melacha carrying the penalty of stoning we rule accordingly.

Radbaz, part 1, siman 282, likewise discusses a child born on Shabbos approximately a quarter-hour before nightfall and writes that, as a matter of halacha, it appears to him that the brit milah should be performed on the following Shabbos, but he did not wish to rule so in practice unless the majority of the sages of Israel agreed, because of the severity of Shabbos desecration.

It appears from his words that his hesitation arose because in his place people accepted Shabbos from sunset. If so, the same issue would arise at the end of Shabbos. In our countries, however, where people sometimes do not accept Shabbos until close to a quarter-hour before nightfall, as explained in siman 261, one may rely upon the accepted calculation for brit milah as well, because the great authorities follow it.

Seif 3, an 8-month child, if, etc. See Shabbos 135a and 136a, and Yevamos 80a-b. Tosafos explain that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages dispute 2 matters. Regarding a child certainly born in the eighth month, the Sages regard him as certainly nonviable and he does not leave that status until the later period discussed by R' Abbahu, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel treats him as doubtful until 30 days and as certainly viable after 30 days. Regarding an ordinary birth of uncertain gestational length, the Sages follow the majority of women and presume the child viable, whereas Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel treats the child as doubtful until 30 days.

The passages in Yevamos and Shabbos must therefore be read together. The case in Yevamos concerns a definite 8-month child, while the case in Shabbos concerns ordinary or doubtful births. This also explains why the authorities distinguish between a child whose hair and nails are fully developed and one whose physical development is incomplete.

With respect to pikuach nefesh, however, even a doubt is sufficient to desecrate Shabbos. This is evident from Erchin, where Shabbos is desecrated in order to attempt to save a fetus after the mother's death. Ran at the end of Yoma likewise indicates that doubts concerning life are treated leniently. Therefore the statements of those who refuse to desecrate Shabbos for every doubtful 8-month child require careful limitation.

The rulings in Even HaEzer concerning a kohen's wife and the need for chalitzah also show that the categories cannot simply be reduced to whether the hair and nails are complete. In cases of ordinary doubtful gestation, the majority presumption of viable births remains significant.

The statements of Tashbatz and Bach that even ordinary newborns do not leave doubtful status until 30 days together with completion of hair and nails require study, because that is not the straightforward view of the Sages. Even according to Tosafos, who explain that R' Yehudah and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel agree in certain aspects of the definite 8-month child, ordinary doubtful births are treated differently.

The halacha therefore depends on whether the case is one of a definite 8-month child, an ordinary child of uncertain gestation, or a child with incomplete physical development. The rules of brit milah and pikuach nefesh follow these distinctions, with doubtful danger treated more leniently than ordinary ritual questions.

Seif katan 3, "and born," etc. One must examine him afterward, because perhaps when the organ becomes erect he will appear as one born without a visible foreskin. If so, although at present, when it is not erect, he does not appear that way, he is nevertheless considered one born in that state, and hatafat dam brit does not override Shabbos.

"And born without a visible foreskin." I found written that it requires study why nowadays the custom is not to examine the child afterward. One must say as Bach writes in Yoreh De'ah, siman 264, that he must appear without a visible foreskin even when the organ is not erect. Accordingly, if he does not appear that way when it is not erect, the brit milah may be performed on Shabbos. This requires study whether one may rely upon this to permit an act involving the severe laws of Shabbos.

Seif katan 4, "2 foreskins," meaning 2 skins one above the other. I saw in Responsa Panim Meirot, part 2, end of siman 31, that he understood these 2 skins as referring to the skins involved in priyah. He therefore wrote that when 2 skins are seen one should not perform the priyah on Shabbos but should wait until after Shabbos. His wording implies that the priyah should be done on Sunday, since even a brit milah not performed at its proper time must be performed by day. Yet the priyah membrane is thin, and if one waits so long it may adhere strongly to the organ and become difficult or impossible to separate, potentially endangering the child or leaving him with an incomplete brit milah.

It therefore appears more correct, in my humble opinion, that "2 skins" means 2 upper foreskins that are ordinarily called skins, whereas the thin membrane separated during priyah is generally called a membrane, although at times it too is called a skin.

One may ask how it can be known before the procedure that there is another skin beneath the upper one. A case is possible where 1 foreskin covers the entire organ and has only the small urinary opening typical of infants, while a second foreskin lies above it and has a much larger opening toward the top. We indeed find infants with only 1 foreskin whose opening is unusually wide at the urinary opening, so that beneath it the organ appears as though there were no visible foreskin. In the case of 2 foreskins, there is 1 ordinary foreskin closed except at the urinary opening, and above it another skin covering the organ but opened widely near the head. In this way one can see that 2 distinct skins require cutting.

"Twilight." See Magen Avraham, who concludes that if the infant was born approximately a quarter-hour before nightfall the matter is doubtful, while if he was born earlier the brit milah is performed on Friday. If he was born on Shabbos approximately a quarter-hour before nightfall, the brit milah is performed on Shabbos according to this calculation.

Radbaz, siman 282, writes that if an infant was born on Friday after sunset but before 3 medium stars were visible, and there is doubt whether the birth occurred before the end of sunset or after it but before the stars appeared, the brit milah is deferred. See also the extensive discussion at the end of Darkei Noam in the treatise Milchamot Mitzvah, Responsa Bach siman 154, and the later authorities.

"Born without a visible foreskin." It requires study why the custom is not to examine afterward. Magen Avraham explains in the name of Bach, Yoreh De'ah siman 264, that the child must appear this way even when the organ is not erect. If he does not appear so in that state, one performs the brit milah on Shabbos. Magen Avraham nevertheless questions whether this is sufficient basis to permit an act involving severe Shabbos laws.

See also Shach at the end of Yoreh De'ah, siman 264, and siman 263 regarding a concealed foreskin. Where actual tissue obstructing the brit milah remains, the mitzvah can override Shabbos under the ordinary rules. Some authorities discuss the case of one born without a visible foreskin and indicate that the drawing of covenantal blood should preferably be done after Shabbos. The Talmud in Shabbos 135 is the principal source and the matter remains subject to the distinctions of the earlier authorities.

Seif 5, "and born without a visible foreskin." This follows Rabbah there, who says that we are concerned for a hidden foreskin, and the halacha follows Rabbah against Rav Yosef.

"And one born by Caesarean section, and a non-Jewish woman," etc., "and one," etc. The ruling remains doubtful because Rav Asi's position differs from the first Tanna. We are uncertain whether Rav Asi had heard the baraita and nevertheless disagreed with the first Tanna, or whether he had not heard the baraita and would have accepted it had he heard it.

"Twilight." See Mishnah Berurah, where I cited Radbaz. This is not treated as a classic double doubt, 1 doubt whether it was still day and another doubt within twilight itself. Pri Megadim suggests that perhaps the mother's prior status as pregnant is relevant, though that presumption is not especially strong for determining the precise halachic time of birth.

Where there is uncertainty whether the head emerged before or during twilight, one cannot automatically say that we establish the mother in her prior status until the later moment. Once the head emerged, the Torah may already regard the child as born. Thus, if a known interval elapsed between emergence of the head and completion of the birth, the timing of the head's emergence must itself be evaluated.

Several authorities discuss a case in which the child was fully born after 3 medium stars were visible, but there was a delay from the emergence of the head. If the witnesses can estimate that the head clearly emerged while it was still day, one follows what they saw. If they cannot determine the time, there is substantial reason to be stringent and not allow the brit milah to override Shabbos.

"Born without a visible foreskin." The term refers to a child who appears so even without erection. If the child appears to have a foreskin when the organ is not erect, but after erection it appears otherwise, the authorities discuss whether this status is considered present from birth. The practical law depends upon whether there is truly hidden foreskin tissue that requires cutting or merely hatafat dam brit.

"Caesarean section." A child removed through the abdominal wall rather than through ordinary birth does not have the same law concerning an eighth-day brit milah overriding Shabbos, because the Scriptural formulation connects the eighth day with the mother's status of birth impurity.

"2 foreskins." The authorities explain this either as 2 organs or as 2 superimposed foreskins. In either interpretation the brit milah does not override Shabbos because of the unresolved doubt concerning the Torah's application to the case.

The common denominator of these cases is uncertainty concerning whether the Torah's ordinary rule of an eighth-day brit milah applies in a form strong enough to override Shabbos. Where the mother's birth does not create tumat leidah, such as Caesarean delivery or a non-Jewish mother who converts only afterward, the exclusion follows the Scriptural relationship between the mother's impurity and the son's eighth day.

"Twilight." The calculation of twilight for brit milah follows the distinctions explained by the authorities concerning sunset and the appearance of 3 medium stars. If a child is born before the doubtful period, the eighth day is counted from that day; if the birth occurs during the doubtful period, the brit milah is deferred because a doubtful brit milah does not override Shabbos.

If the infant's head emerged before nightfall but the full birth occurred after nightfall, one must determine whether the head had emerged sufficiently to constitute birth. Where it is clear from the interval that the head emerged while it was still day, the halachic birth may be attributed to the earlier time. Where the timing is uncertain, one must be stringent.

If, after the full birth, 3 medium stars were seen, this alone does not prove that they were already visible when the head emerged. If only large stars had been visible before, they do not establish night. Where many small stars are already visible, there is stronger basis to treat it as night.

The authorities therefore rule that where there was a perceptible delay between emergence of the head and completion of birth, one cannot simply apply a presumption that the birth occurred only at the later moment. For Torah law, emergence of the head can itself constitute birth. The time of that emergence must therefore be evaluated independently, and if it remains doubtful the brit milah does not override Shabbos.

Seif katan 5, "the scalpel," etc. Rama in Yoreh De'ah understood Rabbeinu Yerucham to permit moving the scalpel after the brit milah, because once it came into one's hand permissibly it may be returned to a place of safekeeping. Magen Avraham, however, cites Rabbeinu Yerucham's language and explains it differently. Maharshal also understood Rabbeinu Yerucham in the lenient manner, yet he goes further and permits moving the scalpel even after it was put down.

The argument that there is no muktzeh for half of Shabbos means that at twilight the scalpel was not muktzeh, because it was needed for the brit milah. Even though after the procedure there is no further need for it, perhaps it should not become muktzeh because during part of Shabbos it was fit for permitted use.

Magen Avraham writes, however, that it appears proper to be stringent. This case is not governed by the principle that there is no muktzeh for half of Shabbos. Yerushalmi, cited in siman 651 regarding a lulav, indicates that once the blessing was recited and the mitzvah fulfilled, after the lulav is put down it is again forbidden to move it. This shows that the principle does not apply to a case of this type.

The rule that there is no muktzeh for half of Shabbos applies where an object temporarily became unfit and later became fit again, such as figs that were moist and edible at twilight, later became unfit while drying, and then completed drying and became edible again. Since they were fit at twilight and later returned to fitness, the temporary interval does not create muktzeh. A brit milah scalpel is different. Its ordinary status is muktzeh machmat chisaron kis. Before the procedure it is permitted only because it is needed for the mitzvah. Afterward it returns to its normal restrictive status.

The same is true of a utensil whose melacha is forbidden. Even though one permissibly used it for its body or place, afterward one may not move it merely from sun to shade. Ramban's ruling concerning burial implements is similar: their continued permissibility depends on the possibility that they may still be needed that day. Once it is known that they will no longer be needed, their ordinary muktzeh status returns.

Maharit writes that because the scalpel is still in the mohel's hand after the brit milah, this itself permits him to carry it to a place of safekeeping. Magen Avraham therefore derives that the leniency applies specifically so long as he has not put it down. Once he puts it down, moving it anew is forbidden.

Taz in Yoreh De'ah, siman 266, gives another reason for leniency. If the mohel had to throw away the scalpel immediately after use, he might refrain from performing the brit milah out of fear that the instrument would be lost. This is stronger than ordinary cases in which the Sages permitted the end of an act because otherwise people would refrain from beginning it. Taz nevertheless limits the leniency to placing the instrument safely in the same room, not carrying it elsewhere when unnecessary.

According to Magen Avraham, however, so long as the scalpel remains in the mohel's hand he may carry it to any place he wishes. Once it has been set down, it may no longer be moved even merely within that room. In a case where 1 mohel performs both the cutting and priyah and must therefore put down the scalpel after the cutting, there is room to permit picking it up again because of the concern that otherwise he may refrain from undertaking the mitzvah. Eliyah Rabbah suggests handing it directly to another person, though it is difficult to understand how this helps, because for the second person this would be a new act of moving muktzeh.

Beit Yosef writes that one may not carry the infant from his house through an unjoined courtyard to the place of the scalpel. The principle that a living person carries himself does not apply to an infant of this age in the relevant way. Through a non-Jew there is room for leniency where no Torah-level public domain is involved. Even so, it is preferable to bring the scalpel to the infant rather than bring the infant to the scalpel, because after the brit milah one would otherwise need a second rabbinic leniency to return the infant to his mother.

Where bringing the infant to the synagogue would require carrying through an unjoined courtyard, it should not be done merely for the honor of performing the brit milah in the synagogue if the procedure can be performed at home. If absolutely necessary and no other method is possible, the authorities discuss reliance upon a non-Jew and the general leniencies of a double rabbinic prohibition for a mitzvah.

"A scalpel from before Shabbos," etc. It is written in Yoreh De'ah, siman 266, that one may move the knife after the brit milah. This is based on Rabbeinu Yerucham, who writes that after the procedure one may return the knife, because once the utensil came into one's hand permissibly he may carry it to any place he wishes; Ramban writes likewise. The intent is the general rule that when one already has a muktzeh object in his hand in a permitted manner, he need not immediately drop it.

Maharshal also permits moving the knife, but he appears to disagree with Rabbeinu Yerucham's limitation and permits it even after it was put down. He relies on the principle that there is no muktzeh for half of Shabbos. It appears to me, however, that one should be stringent. The Yerushalmi cited in siman 651 regarding a lulav shows that after the mitzvah was completed and the lulav was put down, it becomes muktzeh again.

The rule that there is no muktzeh for half of Shabbos applies where the object became temporarily unfit and then returned to fitness, as explained in siman 310. Here the knife's ordinary status is muktzeh machmat chisaron kis. Its permitted use for brit milah does not permanently remove that status. After the procedure, when it is no longer needed, it returns to its ordinary prohibition.

Likewise, a utensil whose melacha is forbidden may be moved for use of its body or place, but afterward one may not move it from sun to shade. Ramban's discussion of burial implements is similar. They remain movable only so long as they may still be needed for another deceased person that day.

Mahari Beit writes that rinsing the scalpel after the brit milah is forbidden when this is done only for preservation after Shabbos, but there is no muktzeh problem while the instrument is still in his hand. One should therefore be stringent not to put it down until he has carried it to a place of safekeeping.

Beit Yosef writes that it is forbidden to carry the infant from his house through a courtyard to the scalpel. Through a non-Jew there is room for leniency where no Torah-level public domain is involved. It is nevertheless clear that one should not bring the infant to the synagogue through an unjoined courtyard merely for the ceremony, since the brit milah can be performed at home. Where there is no alternative, one may rely upon the authorities who permit even stronger forms of non-Jewish assistance for the needs of brit milah.

The following cases of brit milah do not override Shabbos: an androgynos; one born during twilight; one born without a visible foreskin; one delivered by Caesarean section; a child born to a non-Jewish woman who subsequently converted; and one who has 2 foreskins.

(13) "Androgynos." A child who has male genital characteristics and also female genital characteristics. [Rambam, chapter 1 of Hilchot Milah]

(14) "Born during twilight." Whether the twilight was on Friday evening or at the conclusion of Shabbos, the brit milah does not override Shabbos, because the eighth day is uncertain. If the child was definitely born before twilight, the normal eighth-day calculation applies.

(15) "Born without a visible foreskin." This means that even when the organ is not erect he appears to have no visible foreskin. Where he appears ordinary when not erect and only afterward appears otherwise, the authorities discuss whether the case has this status.

(16) "Caesarean section." The mother had difficulty giving birth and the child was removed through the abdominal wall rather than by ordinary delivery.

(17) "2 foreskins." Some explain this as 2 organs, each with a foreskin; others explain that there are 2 distinct skins one above the other.

(18) "Their brit milah does not override Shabbos." The reason in most of these cases is uncertainty: an androgynos is not certainly male; a twilight birth may not have its eighth day on Shabbos; one born without a visible foreskin may not actually have hidden foreskin requiring a Torah-level brit milah; and in the case of 2 foreskins it is unclear how the Torah's rule applies. A Caesarean birth and a child born to a non-Jewish woman who later converts are excluded for another reason: the mother did not have the ordinary tumat leidah status connected by the Torah to the son's eighth-day brit milah.

"And they bathe." One should not soak a sheet, because this is laundering. Rather, a non-Jew may place the sheet into the water. If the hot water spilled, one may tell a non-Jew to bring water that was heated for the non-Jew, but should not tell him to heat water specifically for the infant.

Beit Yosef writes at the end of Yoreh De'ah, siman 267, in the name of Rashbatz, that an infant who had been ill, was not given a brit milah at the proper time, and then recovered should not be given the brit milah on Thursday, lest the third day after the procedure fall on Shabbos and require desecration of Shabbos. The custom was likewise to avoid Friday. See there Shach and Taz, and see Knesset HaGedolah.

Magen Avraham writes that nowadays, when the infant is not ordinarily bathed in the former manner after brit milah, there is no reason for this concern, because it is not common that Shabbos would need to be desecrated on his account. Therefore one should not delay performance of the mitzvah merely for this reason.

"He should not perform the brit milah." Magen Avraham writes that the same applies to one who has performed the cutting but has never performed priyah: he may not perform priyah for the first time on Shabbos, and the reason is the same. See Responsa Chavot Yair, siman 158.

A mohel who comes to perform a brit milah on Shabbos and says that he has already performed 1 procedure on a weekday is believed and need not bring proof. Once he has performed either the cutting or the priyah successfully once, we do not require that he establish proficiency by doing it 3 times. If he were not confident that he could perform it without error, he would not expose himself to the severe possibility of desecrating Shabbos.

The Shulchan Aruch states that even the father may perform the brit milah. One might have thought that the father is different because he certainly desires the resulting repair of his son and the act is therefore a psik reisha beneficial to him, whereas another mohel might be treated differently. The ruling teaches that no such distinction is made.

"Who has never performed a brit milah." It appears to me that the same applies to one who has performed the cutting but has never performed priyah: he may not perform priyah for the first time on Shabbos, and the reason is the same in both cases.
